newsitem.title: UK: Halifax makes blue chip stock market debut.
newsitem.headline: Halifax makes blue chip stock market debut.

text.p: Britain gained a new banking giant on Monday when former building society Halifax Plc made its 18 billion pound ($29.5 billion) London stock exchange debut.
Nearly two million people will have received windfalls of an average 2,417 pounds after around a quarter of Halifax shares were sold at 732.5 pence per share at an auction last Friday.

The shares opened 42 pence higher at 774.5 pence but traded back to 753.5 pence by 0834 GMT. At the auction price a Halifax shareholder with the maximum share entitlement will have collected 10,116 pounds.
"We hope our members will be delighted with the price," Halifax's head of corporate affairs Gary Marsh told Reuters in an interview. "We are pleased to be able to cement our relationship with them."
Analysts had forecast a high opening price at the auction, although they said the price could have been even higher had there not been a fall in shares in the bank sector on Friday.
With a market capitalisation of more than 18 billion pounds, Halifax easily makes the top 10 of Britain's top 100 quoted companies.
At the auction level, which gives it a market capitalisation of 18.4 billion pounds, it slots in at number eight, Marsh said.
The new bank on the block has in fact sneaked in slightly ahead of banking rival Barclays Plc in terms of market capitalisation, he added.
The cash-rich Halifax is widely predicted to give high street banks National Westminster Bank Plc, Lloyds TSB, Midland and Barclays a run for their money.

Marsh declined to comment when asked on whether Halifax, which has around 20 million customers and more than three billion pounds in cash, would use its new-found flexibility as a public company to make a quick acquisition.
But he repeated Halifax would consider going on the acquisition trail. "That is one of the options we are looking at," he said.
Halifax's brokers Merrill Lynch and Cazenove & Co auctioned around 570 million, 23 percent, of the flotation shares to institutional investors keen to pick up a slice of the huge share handout.
Some 7.6 million Halifax members, those individuals who had saved or borrowed with the 144-year-old society, have become shareholders through the flotation.
Around 1.4 million of these have elected to take share certificates, 1.9 million sold at the first auction and others have taken up the Halifax's offer of a special shareholder account.
Those who decided to cash in on their windfall immediately sold through the auction at which they were guaranteed a minimum price of 415 pence.
The Halifax flotation follows last month's float of the Alliance & Leicester which also ditched its mutual status, where it was owned by its members, in favour of becoming a public limited company.
One analyst, who declined to be named, suggested Halifax shares could rise as high as 800 pence but they would not necessarily stay at this level.
"It's possible the shares will trade up to around eight pounds today that's not to say we expect it to stay at that level," he said.
But the shares were likely to trade back to between 6.45 and seven pounds if the market began to ignore the shortage of stock and looked at the fundamentals of the new bank.
"I don't think there is anyone in the market that thinks Halifax is worth 775 pence on fundamentals."
And the Halifax itself is prepared for the trials and tribulations of life as one of Britain's stock market giants.

"We are pleased we have got the reception we have as a quoted company but this is by no means the end of it for the Halifax. Its the end of one chapter but the beginning of a new one," said Halifax's Marsh.
